questions.question: What is sync.Mutex in Go, and when do you need it?
questions.title: Sync Mutex Basics
questions.direct_answer: A mutual-exclusion lock. Lock() blocks until acquired, Unlock() releases. Use when goroutines read AND write shared state — the lock serializes access so only one goroutine is in the critical section.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: A mutual-exclusion lock. Lock() blocks until acquired, Unlock() releases. Use when goroutines read AND write shared state — the lock serializes access so only one goroutine is in the critical section.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    G1[goroutine 1] --> L[Lock] --> CS[critical section] --> U[Unlock]
    G2[goroutine 2] -.->|blocks| L
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The race mechanism: counter++ compiles to load, add, store. Two goroutines can both load 5, both compute 6, both store 6 — two increments, one result. Multiply by 100 goroutines, ~10 overlaps: 90 (verified). The mutex serializes: Lock CASes the state to held (atomic); the critical section runs alone; Unlock wakes the FIFO queue's head. An uncontended Lock is one atomic instruction — nanoseconds.

The critical-section discipline: the section contains exactly the shared-state access, nothing slow (no I/O, no allocations inside — everything inside is serialized). The read-copy-update pattern for slow work: copy under the lock, release, work on the copy.

The copylocks vet check: a struct containing a Mutex passed by value copies the lock state — two goroutines 'holding' the same logical lock. The idioms: methods on the struct (pointer receiver), or embed sync.Mutex.

questions.question: What is the difference between sync.Mutex and sync.RWMutex?
questions.title: When would you use Sync Mutex Basics in a real project
questions.direct_answer: Mutex: one goroutine total. RWMutex: many concurrent READERS, one exclusive WRITER. RWMutex wins when reads vastly outnumber writes and the read section is meaningful.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Sync Mutex Basics.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Mutex: one goroutine total. RWMutex: many concurrent READERS, one exclusive WRITER. RWMutex wins when reads vastly outnumber writes and the read section is meaningful.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The lock shapes:

```go
var m sync.Mutex     // ONE at a time, any access
var rw sync.RWMutex  // RLock: many readers; Lock: one writer

rw.RLock()   // reader — doesn't block other RLocks
rw.RUnlock()
rw.Lock()    // writer — blocks ALL
rw.Unlock()
```

Executed: three concurrent RLocks all entered simultaneously (all 3 printed 'reading'). A Mutex would have serialized them.

RWMutex rules: RLock and RLock coexist. Lock blocks everything. A pending Lock also blocks NEW RLocks (writer priority — anti-starvation).

When RWMutex wins: read-heavy cache (1000 reads per write, meaningful read sections). When it loses: writes frequent (Lock serializes everything — you got Mutex behavior plus complexity) or reads tiny (RLock/RUnlock overhead exceeds the parallelization).

The guidance: start with Mutex (simpler, faster almost always). Switch when profiling shows lock contention on a read-mostly path.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    G1[goroutine 1] --> L[Lock] --> CS[critical section] --> U[Unlock]
    G2[goroutine 2] -.->|blocks| L
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
RWMutex's state machine: a counter (negative = writer holds; positive = reader count) plus a writer-pending flag. RLock increments readers and proceeds (if no writer). Lock sets writer-pending, waits for readers to reach zero, flips to held — new RLocks queue behind (anti-starvation).

The complexity cost: RWMutex's transitions are more work than Mutex's single CAS. An uncontended RLock is fast, but a contended mix produces more scheduling churn than the same workload on a Mutex. Benchmark your actual contention pattern.

The anti-pattern the distinction enables: RLock around a map read is safe for the map structure, but if the value is a pointer, the POINTED-TO data needs its own sync — RLock protects the map, not the pointees. If the 'read' mutates anything (caching into the map), it's a write wearing a read lock.

questions.question: How do you use sync.WaitGroup in Go?
questions.title: a common mistake when using Sync Mutex Basics
questions.direct_answer: wg.Add(1) before spawning, defer wg.Done() inside, wg.Wait() to block until all Done calls have fired. Counter-based: Add increments, Done decrements, Wait blocks at zero.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Sync Mutex Basics.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: wg.Add(1) before spawning, defer wg.Done() inside, wg.Wait() to block until all Done calls have fired. Counter-based: Add increments, Done decrements, Wait blocks at zero.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The WaitGroup is the join primitive:

```go
var wg sync.WaitGroup
for i := 1; i <= 3; i++ {
    wg.Add(1)
    go func(n int) {
        defer wg.Done()   // fires when this goroutine returns
        work(n)
    }(i)
}
wg.Wait()   // blocks until counter = 0
fmt.Println("all done")
```

Executed: workers 1, 2, 3 finished in order (simulated with delays), then 'all done'.

The three methods:
- Add(n): increments. BEFORE the spawn (Add after go is a race).
- Done(): decrements by 1. defer wg.Done() — runs on every exit path.
- Wait(): blocks until 0. Multiple goroutines can Wait on the same group.

The reuse rule: after Wait returns, the WaitGroup is reusable (counter is 0). Add while Wait is active is the classic deadlock.

The standard use is fan-out/fan-in: spawn N with Add(1), collect via channel or shared slice under mutex, Wait, then use the results.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    G1[goroutine 1] --> L[Lock] --> CS[critical section] --> U[Unlock]
    G2[goroutine 2] -.->|blocks| L
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The counter mechanics: WaitGroup is a single integer plus a semaphore. Add atomically increments; Done decrements and signals at zero; Wait parks on the semaphore until signaled. No goroutine-identity tracking — 'N completions,' anonymous and composable.

The ordering bug interviewers probe — Add inside the spawned goroutine:
```go
for i := 0; i < N; i++ {
    go func() { wg.Add(1); defer wg.Done(); work() }()  // BUG
}
wg.Wait()
```
Main might reach Wait before ANY spawned goroutine reaches Add — counter was 0 when Wait checked, Wait returns immediately, results aren't ready. The fix: Add before go — the happens-before chain: Add → spawn → work → Done → 0 → Wait wakes.

The nested pattern: one WaitGroup per 'barrier' — a set of work that must complete before the next phase — with channels carrying the results. WaitGroups compose via counting, not nesting.
